# HabitToll

> HabitToll is an app blocker for iPhone and Android. Walk away for free, or buy 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29. No subscription.

HabitToll ("Put a price on your scroll.") is made by Comads OÜ, Tallinn, Estonia. Contact: help@habittoll.com.

## Facts
- Platforms: iPhone with iOS 26.4 or later (App Store); Android 8 or later (Google Play).
- Price: free to download. Walking away ("Not worth it") is always one tap and free. An unlock is a one-time in-app purchase of 10 minutes at a price the person sets, from €0.29 (other countries see their store's price). No subscription, no ads.
- Optional rules: each further unlock on the same day can cost double, up to 10 times the price (it starts fresh at 04:00); a monthly limit (past it, HabitToll asks before every paid unlock, and "Stop at my limit" stops paid unlocks until the 1st); free minutes each day; 2 free emergency unlocks a month; a settings lock that makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner's code.
- Friends: friends see what you pay each day and your streak, never which apps.
- Privacy: no account. Which apps you block, and how long you use them, never leave the phone.
- Languages: English, German, Spanish. For adults (18 and older).
- Released: App Store on 4 October 2026, Google Play on 14 October 2026.

## FAQ
### Is HabitToll free?
Downloading it is free, and so is the blocking: walking away is always one tap and costs nothing. You only pay when an app is worth it to you: 10 minutes at the price you picked, from €0.29, as a single in-app purchase. There's no subscription.

### How much does an unlock cost?
You choose: from €0.29 for 10 minutes (other countries see their store's price). If you like, each further unlock on the same day costs double, up to 10 times your price, and past your monthly limit HabitToll asks before every paid unlock. You also get two free emergency unlocks a month.

### Who gets the money?
Taxes and the store's share come off first. The rest goes to Comads OÜ, the small company in Tallinn, Estonia, that makes HabitToll, and pays for building the app, its servers, support and ads. Where your money goes

### Does HabitToll work on Android?
Yes. HabitToll is on the App Store for iPhone (iOS 26.4 or later) and on Google Play for Android phones (Android 8 or later), in English, German and Spanish.

### How is it different from Screen Time?
Screen Time counts minutes: it gives apps a daily allowance and a schedule, and a passcode protects the settings, but if you set the passcode yourself, you know it. HabitToll asks “worth it?” when you open an app you picked: walking away is one tap, and going in costs the price you set. If you want it to stick, the settings lock makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need your partner's code. More side by side: HabitToll vs Screen Time and the best app blockers of 2026.

### Can I turn it off?
Yes, you're never locked in. Remove apps, lower your price or stop blocking in Settings, or delete the app. With the settings lock on, easier changes wait 24 hours or need your partner's code.

### What does HabitToll know about me?
Which apps you block, and how long you use them, never leave your phone. There's no account: HabitToll never asks for your name, email, Apple Account or Google Account. Privacy policy

### Who is it for?
Adults who want to open certain apps less often, and decide each time. You must be 18 or older to use HabitToll.

## Help

https://habittoll.com/help/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/hilfe/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/ayuda/

The questions people ask most. Anything else: <help@habittoll.com>

### I need an app right now

Tap **Emergency?** on the pay screen (on Android, on the block screen). It opens free for 10 minutes, twice a month, and works even when your limit is reached.

Keep Phone, Messages and Maps off your list.

### It locked too early

iOS sometimes locks an app before your minutes are up. If it locks a paid unlock again less than 9 minutes after it started, your next unlock is free. Nothing to do.

On Android, an unlock is 10 minutes of use within the hour, and only time with the app in front counts. After the hour it locks, even with minutes left.

Paid, but nothing opened? In HabitToll: Settings → Help → It locked too early → Restore purchases.

### Why is it locked until the 1st?

**Stop at my limit** is on, and your monthly limit is reached. Emergency unlocks still work. To change it, turn off Stop at my limit in Settings → Monthly limit.

### It stopped blocking

Some Android phones stop apps in the background to save battery. In HabitToll: Settings → Help → It stopped blocking → Keep it running. Then check the three switches on Home.

### How do I stop?

You're never locked in. Remove apps or lower your price in Settings; with the settings lock on, easier changes wait 24 hours. Or remove HabitToll's Screen Time access in the iPhone's Settings (on Android: its usage access in Android Settings), or delete the app.

### Refunds

On iPhone, Apple decides refunds. In HabitToll: Settings → Help → Refunds → Request a refund. Or at [reportaproblem.apple.com](https://reportaproblem.apple.com).

On Android, Google Play decides. Find the purchase in your [Google Play order history](https://play.google.com/store/account/orderhistory), then tap Request a refund.

A refund never locks you out and never raises your price.

### New phone?

No account needed. Restore your new iPhone from an iCloud or computer backup, or your new Android phone from your Google backup: your history, streak and prepaid unlocks come with it.

On iPhone, if your apps are missing, pick them again in Settings. On Android, open HabitToll and tap “Blocking is paused. Tap to fix.” to turn the three switches on again.

### What HabitToll can see

On iPhone, Apple gives HabitToll only coded tokens for the apps you block; iOS itself draws their names and icons. On Android, usage access shows HabitToll which app is in front. Which apps you block, and how long you use them, never leave your phone. [Privacy policy](https://habittoll.com/privacy/)

### What you need

An iPhone with iOS 26.4 or later, and Screen Time access for HabitToll. Or an Android phone with Android 8 or later, and usage access and display over other apps for HabitToll. It asks for them during setup.

Write to us

[help@habittoll.com](mailto:help@habittoll.com)

We usually answer within two working days. Never send us your passcode or partner code.

## Where your money goes

https://habittoll.com/money/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/geld/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/dinero/

Your unlocks pay for HabitToll. Here is where the money goes.

### From every unlock

Taxes and the store's share come off first: VAT goes to the state, and Apple or Google keep their share for the store and the payment.

The rest goes to Comads OÜ, the small company in Tallinn, Estonia, that makes HabitToll. It pays for building the app, its servers and support, and ads that bring HabitToll to more people.

### You decide what it costs

You pick the price of 10 minutes and a monthly limit. Walking away is free, two emergency unlocks a month are free, and the best days cost nothing.

Our pledge

### Half of HabitToll's profit funds tree planting with [Tree-Nation](https://tree-nation.com/).

Profit is what's left after all HabitToll's costs, including the ads that bring it to more people, so while we grow and make up earlier losses, it may be small or zero. We pay at least once a year and publish the numbers and the receipt here after every payment.

### Why not with every unlock?

Because an unlock should cost you something. If part of every unlock went to trees, paying could start to feel like doing good, and HabitToll would stop helping you use your phone less. So an unlock buys you 10 minutes, not a donation, and we fund the trees from our profit instead.

### So far

From HabitToll's profit so far  
€0

Next report  
June 2027

### How we count

**Profit** is HabitToll's own result for the calendar year: what Apple and Google pay us for HabitToll, minus everything HabitToll costs, including building it, servers, support, ads, and its share of our company's shared costs (split by revenue). Before income tax.

A year with a loss means nothing to pay for that year, and earlier losses are made up first: we pay half of what's left after that.

We pay at least once a year: half of a year's profit by the end of the following June, once our accounts are done, and earlier or more often when we can. After every payment we publish here what HabitToll earned and spent, the amount, and Tree-Nation's receipt.

Trees count as funded until Tree-Nation confirms they are planted.

If we ever change this pledge, it changes only for years that haven't started, and we say so here first.

### Who we are

Comads OÜ, Ahtri tn 12, 15551 Tallinn, Estonia. Registry code 17276947.

### How it works

1.  You pick the apps you open too often, and a price for 10 minutes, from €0.29.
2.  When you open one of them, HabitToll asks “Worth it?”
3.  Not worth it: one tap, free, and it counts as a walk-away. Worth it: 10 minutes at your price, then it asks again.
4.  The home screen shows how often you walked away this month, your streak and your monthly bill.

### Getting the details right

- An unlock is a purchase of time: 10 minutes, when an app is worth it to the person. Walking away is always free.
- A normal unlock costs the price the person chose. The stores list much higher prices because each further unlock on the same day can cost double, up to 10 times that price, for people who turn that on.
- Past their monthly limit, HabitToll asks before every paid unlock. With “Stop at my limit” on, nothing can be bought until the 1st.
- The “9 years” in the sign-up is each person's own estimate from their answers, not a result of using HabitToll.
- Which apps someone blocks, and how long they use them, never leave the phone. Friends see what someone pays each day and their streak, never which apps.
- HabitToll is for adults. It isn't a parental control app.

## How to block apps on iPhone, for certain hours or for good

https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-iphone/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/apps-sperren-iphone/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/bloquear-apps-iphone/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 21 October 2026

On iPhone, Screen Time does it. On iOS 27, Time Allowances give categories like Social Media a daily amount, and a Screen Time Schedule sets the hours when apps can be used; on iOS 26 the same tools are called App Limits and Downtime. A Screen Time passcode protects the settings. If you’d rather decide each time, an app like HabitToll asks first.

### 1. Turn on Screen Time

Open Settings → Screen Time → Manage Screen Time, and tap Turn On App & Website Activity. Your daily average and the apps you use most then show under Screen Time.

### 2. Give a category a daily amount (Time Allowances)

1.  Open Settings → Screen Time → Time Allowances.
2.  Set a daily total for the phone with the slider, or the minus and plus buttons.
3.  Tap a category, like Social Media, Entertainment or Games, and set its own daily time.
4.  To add a category, tap Manage Categories, then the add button.

Apps in a category work until that category’s allowance or the daily total runs out. If you only want the allowances to apply during certain hours, turn on Match Screen Time Schedule.

App by app: [Instagram](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-instagram/), [TikTok](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-tiktok/) and [YouTube Shorts](https://habittoll.com/guides/limit-youtube-shorts/).

### 3. Set the hours for apps (Screen Time Schedule)

1.  Open Settings → Screen Time → Screen Time Schedule, and turn on Schedule.
2.  Tap Add Schedule, choose the days, and tap Done.
3.  Tap a time window, like Evening, to change its start and end, and choose which categories are allowed in it.

Apps under Always Allowed work at any time. Add them in Settings → Screen Time → Always Allowed: people you always want to reach, and apps like Phone or Maps.

### 4. Protect the settings with a passcode

Open Settings → Screen Time → Manage Screen Time → Lock Screen Time Settings, and enter a four-digit code twice. From then on, the code is needed to change the Screen Time settings you chose. Set up Screen Time Passcode Recovery too, so a forgotten code can be reset with an Apple Account.

If you set the code yourself, you know it, so it stops other people more than it stops you: [why your own passcode is easy to get around](https://habittoll.com/guides/screen-time-passcode/).

### On iOS 26

The same tools have their earlier names:

- **App Limits** (Settings → Screen Time → App Limits → Add Limit): choose categories, or tap a category to pick single apps, tap Next, and set the time. Customize Days gives each day its own time. Apple notes that a limit can be ignored once it’s reached, unless you block it.
- **Downtime** (Settings → Screen Time → Downtime): turn on Scheduled, every day or by day, with start and end times. With a Screen Time passcode set, Block at Downtime appears: then apps outside Always Allowed can’t be opened during Downtime, and show dimmed with an hourglass.
- **Passcode**: Settings → Screen Time → Lock Screen Time Settings.

### When a hard block is too much

If you keep switching Screen Time off because a hard block feels too strict, or keep giving yourself more time, there’s a middle way: a pause with a price.

- HabitToll asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open, single apps or websites.
- Walking away is one tap and free.
- Going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29.
- You can block always, or only at the times you pick, and give a group of apps free minutes a day or free hours, like 20:00 to 21:00.
- Its settings lock makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code.

### Which to use

| You want | Use |
|----|----|
| A daily amount for social media or games | Time Allowances (App Limits on iOS 26) |
| Apps closed at night or at work | A Screen Time Schedule (Downtime on iOS 26) |
| Settings you can’t change in the moment | A Screen Time passcode someone else keeps |
| A decision at every open, not a countdown | HabitToll |

### Questions

#### Can I block a single app instead of a whole category?

On iOS 26, yes: in App Limits → Add Limit, tap a category and pick the app inside it. On iOS 27, Apple describes Time Allowances by category. HabitToll lets you pick single apps and websites on both.

#### What changed in iOS 27?

Apple renamed and rebuilt the tools: App Limits are now Time Allowances, set by category, and Downtime is now part of the Screen Time Schedule, made of time windows. The passcode stayed: Lock Screen Time Settings.

#### What does Block at Downtime do?

It decides what Downtime does on iOS 26. With Block at Downtime on, apps outside Always Allowed can’t be opened during Downtime: they show dimmed with an hourglass. With it off, you see a reminder that it’s Downtime, but you can keep using the apps. You can choose it once a Screen Time passcode is set: Settings → Screen Time → Downtime → Block at Downtime. On iOS 27, Downtime is part of the Screen Time Schedule, and Apple’s guide shows no such switch there.

#### How do I block apps on iPhone for a while, say until tomorrow?

On iOS 26: Settings → Screen Time → Downtime → Turn On Downtime Until Tomorrow (App & Website Activity has to be on). With Block at Downtime on, apps outside Always Allowed then can’t be opened until tomorrow; without it, Downtime is a reminder and you can keep using the apps. On iOS 27, Apple’s guide shows no such switch for your own iPhone: a time window in the Screen Time Schedule sets the hours instead.

*Steps from Apple’s iPhone User Guide for iOS 27 and iOS 26, checked on 16 October 2026 (the last two answers on 21 October 2026).*

## How to block apps on Android, for certain hours or for good

https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-android/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/apps-sperren-android/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/bloquear-apps-android/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 17 October 2026

On Android, Digital Wellbeing does it: an app timer for a daily limit, Focus mode to pause apps during set hours, Bedtime mode for the night, and a PIN to protect your timers. A PIN you set yourself is one you know, so if you want a decision in front of each open instead, an app like HabitToll adds one.

### 1. Give an app a daily limit (app timer)

1.  Open Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers.
2.  Tap Set timer next to the app, choose the time per day, and tap OK.

When the time is up, the app closes and its icon dims for the rest of the day. Timers reset at midnight. To use the app again before then, open the same screen and delete the timer.

App by app: [Instagram](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-instagram/), [TikTok](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-tiktok/) and [YouTube Shorts](https://habittoll.com/guides/limit-youtube-shorts/).

### 2. Pause apps during set hours (Focus mode)

1.  Open Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Focus mode.
2.  Choose the apps to pause.
3.  Tap Turn on now, or Set a schedule with days and times.

While Focus mode is on, you can’t use those apps and you get no notifications from them. Take a break lets you unpause them for a time you choose.

### 3. Wind down at night (Bedtime mode)

Open Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Bedtime mode → Bedtime routine, and choose Use a schedule or Turn on while charging. Bedtime mode can turn on Do Not Disturb and change the screen, for example to Grayscale. It’s made for quieter nights; to pause apps at night, pair it with Focus mode.

### 4. Protect your timers with a PIN

Digital Wellbeing can lock app timers behind a PIN: open Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App limits → App limits PIN, turn on PIN for app time limits, confirm with your phone’s screen lock, and choose a four-digit PIN. Changing a timer then needs the PIN.

As with the iPhone’s Screen Time passcode, a PIN you choose yourself is one you know. Let someone else choose it, or use a waiting time instead.

### On a Samsung Galaxy

Samsung phones have Samsung’s own Digital Wellbeing, and some menus differ from the steps above:

- **App timer:** Settings → Digital Wellbeing and parental controls → App timers → Apps and app categories. Pick the app, tap Add schedule, set the days and the time, and tap Save. On older versions, pick the app and tap Set timer. When the time is up, the app can’t be used for the rest of the day.
- **Apps paused at set hours:** Focus mode has moved to Settings → Modes and Routines. Add a mode (Add mode → Custom), choose when it turns on, and under Stay focused, turn on Restrict app usage.
- **At night:** Bedtime mode is now called Sleep, also under Modes and Routines.
- **A PIN:** Samsung’s help describes a PIN for children’s accounts, not one for your own app timers.

### 5. When you keep switching it off

HabitToll on Android puts a question instead of a timer in front of the apps you pick. It asks “worth it?”: walking away is free, and going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29. Its settings lock makes easier changes, like removing an app or lowering the price, wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code. You can also give a group of apps free minutes a day or free hours, like 20:00 to 21:00.

### What HabitToll needs on Android

- Usage access, to see which app is in front.
- Display over other apps, to show the “worth it?” screen.
- Notifications, to tell you when time is up (optional).

Which apps you block, and how long you use them, never leave your phone.

### Questions

#### Do app timers work on Samsung and other phones?

Yes. Samsung Galaxy phones have Samsung’s own Digital Wellbeing, with the menus described above under “On a Samsung Galaxy”. On phones from other makers, Google notes that the steps can vary by device.

#### What happens at midnight?

App timers reset, and apps that were closed by their timer open again.

*Steps from Google’s Android and Pixel help for Digital Wellbeing, checked on 16 October 2026, and from Samsung’s support pages, checked on 17 October 2026.*

## How to stop doomscrolling, especially at night

https://habittoll.com/guides/stop-doomscrolling/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/doomscrolling-stoppen/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/dejar-el-doomscrolling/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 16 October 2026

Doomscrolling is reading one more post, then another, long after you meant to stop. What helps is rarely willpower in the moment. It’s setting things up beforehand, so the next scroll takes a decision.

### Why it’s hard to stop

A feed has no last page: there’s always one more post. Each open is quick and feels like a small choice, so the total only shows up later, in your Screen Time or Digital Wellbeing numbers. That’s why most of what helps happens before you pick up the phone, not while you’re scrolling.

### 1. Look at your numbers once

On iPhone, open Settings → Screen Time and tap Daily Average. On Android, open Settings → Digital Wellbeing. Find the two or three apps with the most time. Those are the ones to work on; the rest can stay as they are.

### 2. Give the evening a cut-off time

Pick a time after which those apps stay closed, and let the phone hold you to it: a Screen Time Schedule on iPhone (Downtime on iOS 26), Focus mode or Bedtime mode on Android. Step by step: [block apps for certain hours on iPhone](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-iphone/) or [on Android](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-android/).

### 3. Charge the phone outside the bedroom

If the phone isn’t within reach, scrolling in bed starts with getting up. A simple alarm clock takes over the phone’s alarm.

### 4. Turn off notifications from the feeds

Every notification is an invitation to open the app. Keep them for people, like messages and calls, and turn them off for feeds and suggestions.

### 5. Move the apps off your home screen

Put them in a folder on the last page, or remove them from the home screen and open them through search. A few seconds of extra effort are often enough to notice what you’re about to do.

### 6. Put a pause in front of the app

A pause before an app opens turns an automatic open into a decision. A limit you can wave away in a tap is easy to get past. Some apps add a breathing exercise first. HabitToll asks “worth it?”: walking away is one tap and free, and going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set yourself.

### 7. Decide in advance what’s worth it

“Ten minutes after dinner” is a plan; “just checking” isn’t. Decide when an app is worth opening before the moment comes, and the moment gets easier.

### 8. Count the times you don’t open it

The scrolls you skip are invisible unless something counts them. A tally, a streak or a note at the end of the day makes them visible. HabitToll counts every walk-away and keeps a streak of the days you didn’t pay to open an app.

### 9. Tell someone

Saying it out loud to a friend makes it more real, and gives them a reason to ask how it’s going. In HabitToll, friends can see what you pay each day and your streak, never which apps.

### Questions

#### What is doomscrolling?

Scrolling through a feed for much longer than you meant to, often late at night and often through news or posts you don’t enjoy. The word is informal; there’s no strict definition.

#### Do I need an app to stop?

No. Steps 1 to 5 use only what’s already on your phone. An app helps when the built-in limits are too easy to ignore, or too strict to keep.

## How to reduce your screen time: 10 practical steps

https://habittoll.com/guides/reduce-screen-time/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/bildschirmzeit-reduzieren/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/reducir-tiempo-de-pantalla/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 21 October 2026

Start with the two or three apps that take most of your time, not with all of them. Give them a limit or a pause, change what makes you open them, and check your numbers once a week.

### 1. Read your numbers

Your phone already counts. On iPhone: Settings → Screen Time, then tap Daily Average. On Android: Settings → Digital Wellbeing. Note your daily average and the apps on top.

### 2. Pick two or three apps

Most screen time comes from a handful of apps. Working on those few is easier to keep up than limiting everything, and it leaves the useful apps alone: maps, messages, banking.

### 3. Decide what you want instead

“Less phone” is vague. “Read before bed” or “no phone at dinner” is something you can do. Pick one or two moments you want back.

### 4. Give each app a limit or a time

A daily amount (Time Allowances on iPhone, App Limits on iOS 26, app timers on Android) caps the total. Set hours (a Screen Time Schedule on iPhone, Downtime on iOS 26, Focus mode on Android) keep apps closed when you want them closed. Step by step: [iPhone](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-iphone/) · [Android](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-android/).

App by app: [Instagram](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-instagram/), [TikTok](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-tiktok/) and [YouTube Shorts](https://habittoll.com/guides/limit-youtube-shorts/).

### 5. Make the limit hard to wave away

A limit you can change or dismiss in a moment is a reminder, not a limit. On iPhone, a Screen Time passcode that someone else keeps protects your settings; on Android, Digital Wellbeing’s App limits PIN does the same for timers. [Why your own passcode is easy to get around](https://habittoll.com/guides/screen-time-passcode/).

### 6. Or put a price on it

If a hard block feels too strict and a reminder too weak, there’s a middle way: a small price, set by you, to open the app. HabitToll asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open. Walking away is free; 10 minutes cost a price you set, from €0.29, and if you like, the price doubles with each unlock that day.

### 7. Turn off most notifications

Keep notifications from people and turn off the rest. Fewer pings mean fewer reasons to pick up the phone.

### 8. Change the home screen

Move the apps you want to open less off the first page, into a folder or out of sight. Leave the useful ones in front.

### 9. Make one place phone-free

The dinner table, the bedroom or the first half hour of the day. A charger in the hallway does more than a rule you have to remember.

### 10. Check once a week

Look at your numbers on the same day each week. Keep what worked, drop what didn’t, and pick the next app.

### Questions

#### How much screen time is normal?

There’s no single right number, and it depends on what the time is for. A useful question is whether you’re spending it the way you’d choose to.

#### Is it better to delete the apps?

Deleting works for some people, but the app is one download away. A limit, a pause or a price keeps the app for when it’s worth it and adds a decision for the rest.

#### Can I turn off the weekly Screen Time report?

Apple’s iPhone guide shows no switch for the weekly report alone. It arrives as a notification you can tap to see your summary. On iOS 26, turning off App & Website Activity stops the reports, but it also turns off Downtime, App Limits and Always Allowed.

#### How do I turn off Screen Time?

On iOS 27: Settings → Screen Time → Manage Screen Time → Turn Off App & Website Activity. On iOS 26: Settings → Screen Time, scroll down and tap Turn Off App & Website Activity; Apple notes that this also turns off reporting, Downtime, App Limits and Always Allowed. If a Screen Time passcode is set, it must be entered before your Screen Time settings can change. If you’re turning it off because a hard block feels too strict, there’s a middle way: a pause with a price, like HabitToll’s.

*iPhone steps from Apple’s iPhone User Guide for iOS 27 and iOS 26, checked on 21 October 2026.*

## An app blocker you can’t just switch off: your options

https://habittoll.com/guides/app-blocker-you-cant-turn-off/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/app-blocker-nicht-ausschaltbar/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/bloqueador-apps-que-no-se-desactiva/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 16 October 2026

Honest answer first: no app blocker on your own phone is impossible to switch off, because you can always delete it or take away its access. What works is making the way out slow enough that you don’t take it in the moment.

### Why blockers get switched off

Most limits fail in the same moment: the app is blocked, you want it now, and the off switch is two taps away. The fix isn’t a stronger lock you can’t open; it’s putting time or another person between you and the switch, so the decision waits until the urge has passed.

### Option 1: a passcode someone else keeps

On iPhone, Screen Time can lock its own settings with a passcode. If you set it yourself, you know it, so it stops very little. If a friend or partner sets it and keeps it, ending a limit means asking them. [More on the Screen Time passcode](https://habittoll.com/guides/screen-time-passcode/).

### Option 2: a waiting time

A delay on easier settings works without anyone else: any change that loosens your rules only takes effect a day later. Tightening still works at once. In HabitToll, the settings lock does this: removing apps, lowering your price or stopping the blocking waits 24 hours.

### Option 3: a partner’s code

Instead of the waiting time, HabitToll’s settings lock can use a code from a person you choose. Easier changes then need their code, or they wait. They never see your apps; they only hold the code.

### Option 4: a price instead of a wall

A lock you can’t open makes people look for the way around it. A small price, set by you, takes away the reason: when an app is worth it, you pay and go in; when it isn’t, walking away costs nothing. HabitToll works this way, with 10 minutes from €0.29 and two free emergency unlocks a month.

### What no app can stop

On your own phone you can always delete a blocker, or remove its Screen Time access on iPhone or its usage access on Android. That’s true for every blocker, HabitToll included: its terms say that taking away its access, or deleting it, always ends the blocking.

### Questions

#### Is a physical blocker better?

Some people like a separate device you have to tap to unlock apps. It adds a step in the real world, which can help; it also means carrying or leaving the device somewhere. The same idea applies: the more effort the way out takes, the less often you take it.

#### Can I make it permanent?

Not on your own phone, and that’s on purpose: you stay in control. What you can choose is how slow and how deliberate the way out is.

## A Screen Time passcode for yourself: why it’s easy to get around, and what helps

https://habittoll.com/guides/screen-time-passcode/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/bildschirmzeit-code/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/codigo-tiempo-de-uso/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 16 October 2026

A Screen Time passcode stops anyone else from changing your Screen Time settings. If you set it yourself, it rarely stops you, because you know it. To make your limits stick, let someone else keep the code, add a waiting time, or replace the wall with a price.

### What the passcode does

With a Screen Time passcode, the code is needed before anyone can change the Screen Time settings you chose: your allowances, your schedule, or Screen Time itself. On iOS 26 it also unlocks Block at Downtime, which makes Downtime a real block instead of a reminder.

### How to set it

1.  Open Settings → Screen Time → Manage Screen Time. On iOS 26, scroll down in Settings → Screen Time instead.
2.  Tap Lock Screen Time Settings and enter a four-digit code twice.
3.  Set up Screen Time Passcode Recovery, so the code can be reset with an Apple Account if it’s forgotten.

### Why it rarely stops you

When you set the code yourself, it’s in your head. In the moment you want the app, four digits are quick to type, and the limit turns back into a reminder. A passcode is a lock against other people, not against yourself.

### Three ways to make your limits stick

#### 1. Let someone else keep the code

Hand your phone to someone you trust at step 2, and let them choose the code without showing you. Apple’s recovery uses the Apple Account entered when the code was set up, which can be someone else’s: if they enter their own account there, resetting the code needs them too. More time then always means asking them.

#### 2. Add a waiting time

A rule that loosens only a day later gives the urge time to pass. Screen Time has no waiting time, but HabitToll’s settings lock does: removing apps, lowering your price or stopping the blocking waits 24 hours, while tightening works at once.

#### 3. Replace the wall with a price

A wall makes you look for the way around it. HabitToll asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open: walking away is free, and going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29. There’s no code to type; the decision is the price.

### Questions

#### What if I forget my Screen Time passcode?

Open Settings → Screen Time → Manage Screen Time → Change Screen Time Passcode, tap Change Screen Time Passcode again, and enter the Apple Account that was used for recovery when the code was set up. Then choose a new code.

#### Is the Screen Time passcode the same as my iPhone passcode?

No. It’s a separate four-digit code, only for Screen Time.

*Steps from Apple’s iPhone User Guide and Apple Support, checked on 16 October 2026.*

## How to block Instagram or give it a time limit, on iPhone and Android

https://habittoll.com/guides/block-instagram/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/instagram-sperren/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/bloquear-instagram/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 17 October 2026

Instagram’s own Daily limit only reminds you; for adults it doesn’t lock the app. A limit that closes Instagram comes from the phone: Screen Time on iPhone and an app timer in Digital Wellbeing on Android, best with a passcode or PIN. If you’d rather decide at each open, HabitToll asks “worth it?” before Instagram opens.

### 1. Instagram’s Daily limit (a reminder)

1.  In Instagram, open your profile and tap the menu, top right.
2.  Under How you use Instagram, tap Time management, then Daily limit.
3.  Choose an amount of time.

After that much time on Instagram in a day, a reminder appears. The app stays open: only the parent of a supervised Teen Account can block Instagram when a limit is reached. The Daily limit works in the app, not on a computer. Time management also shows how much time you spent on Instagram a day, on average, over the last 7 days.

Sleep mode, in the same place, pauses notifications at the times you choose and sends an auto-reply to messages. Instagram itself stays usable.

### 2. On iPhone: Screen Time

**On iOS 27:**

1.  Open Settings → Screen Time → Time Allowances.
2.  Tap Social Media and set its daily time.
3.  To see which apps a category holds, tap Manage Categories, then the category. Apple’s guide to Time Allowances says categories can be added and their apps changed.

For set hours, add a Screen Time Schedule: Settings → Screen Time → Screen Time Schedule.

**On iOS 26:**

1.  Open Settings → Screen Time → App Limits → Add Limit.
2.  Tap a category to see its apps, select Instagram, tap Next and set the time.

Apple notes that, by default, a limit can be ignored once it’s reached. With a Screen Time passcode set, Block at Downtime keeps apps closed during Downtime.

**The passcode:** Settings → Screen Time → Manage Screen Time → Lock Screen Time Settings (on iOS 26, Settings → Screen Time → Lock Screen Time Settings). If you set it yourself, you know it: [why your own passcode is easy to get around](https://habittoll.com/guides/screen-time-passcode/).

### 3. On Android: an app timer

1.  Open Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers.
2.  Tap Set timer next to Instagram, choose the time per day and tap OK.

When the time is up, Instagram closes and its icon dims for the rest of the day. Timers reset at midnight. So that the timer isn’t simply deleted, set a PIN: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App limits → App limits PIN. On a Samsung Galaxy the menus are named differently: [how to block apps on Android](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-android/) has both.

### 4. Instagram in the browser

Instagram also works at instagram.com, and a limit on the app doesn’t always cover it.

- **Android:** Digital Wellbeing has a separate site timer for Chrome. In Digital Wellbeing, tap the chart, then Chrome and Show sites, and tap Set site timer next to instagram.com.
- **iPhone:** on iOS 27, a Time Allowance covers an app’s website when the app declares that website as its own. On iOS 26 you can block the address completely: Settings → Screen Time → Content & Privacy Restrictions → App Store, Media, Web, & Games → Web Content → Limit Adult Websites, then Add Website under Never Allow.

### When a limit is too easy to switch off

If you keep dismissing the reminder or deleting the timer, a question with a price is a middle way:

- HabitToll asks “worth it?” before Instagram opens, and on iPhone before instagram.com too.
- Walking away is one tap and free.
- Going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29; then it asks again.
- You can block always, or only at the times you pick, and give a group of apps, like Instagram and TikTok, free minutes a day or free hours.
- Its settings lock makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code.

### Which to use

| You want | Use |
|----|----|
| A nudge after a while on Instagram | Instagram’s Daily limit |
| A daily amount that closes the app | Screen Time (iPhone) or an app timer (Android) |
| Instagram closed at night or at work | A Screen Time Schedule (Downtime on iOS 26), or Focus mode on Android |
| A decision at every open, not a countdown | HabitToll |

### Questions

#### Why doesn’t Instagram’s daily limit stop me?

For adults it’s a reminder: it appears after the time you chose, and the app stays open. Only the parent of a supervised Teen Account can block Instagram at the limit. For a limit that closes the app, use Screen Time on iPhone or an app timer on Android.

#### Can I block Instagram only at certain hours?

Yes. On iPhone, a Screen Time Schedule sets when categories can be used (on iOS 26, Downtime with Block at Downtime and a passcode). On Android, Focus mode pauses Instagram on a schedule. HabitToll can ask only at the times you pick.

*Steps from Instagram’s Help Center, Apple’s iPhone User Guide for iOS 27 and iOS 26, and Google’s Android help for Digital Wellbeing, checked on 17 October 2026. Menus can differ by app version and phone.*

## How to block TikTok or give it a time limit, on iPhone and Android

https://habittoll.com/guides/block-tiktok/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/tiktok-sperren/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/bloquear-tiktok/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 17 October 2026

TikTok’s own Daily screen time tells you when your time is up, and for adults a code on the screen lets you carry on. A limit that closes TikTok comes from the phone: Screen Time on iPhone and an app timer in Digital Wellbeing on Android, best with a passcode or PIN. If you’d rather decide at each open, HabitToll asks “worth it?” before TikTok opens.

### 1. TikTok’s Daily screen time

1.  In TikTok, open your profile and tap the menu ☰.
2.  Tap Settings and privacy → Time and well-being → Screen time.
3.  Turn on Daily screen time and choose a limit.

When you reach it, TikTok tells you, and you either close the app or enter the code shown on the screen to go back. The limit belongs to your account: it applies in the app and on tiktok.com, the time counts both together, and on the web you can set a different limit for each day.

In the same place, Sleep hours mute push notifications at night and show a reminder to take a break, and weekly screen time updates compare your week with the one before.

### 2. On iPhone: Screen Time

**On iOS 27:**

1.  Open Settings → Screen Time → Time Allowances.
2.  Tap Social Media and set its daily time.
3.  To see which apps a category holds, tap Manage Categories, then the category. Apple’s guide to Time Allowances says categories can be added and their apps changed.

For set hours, add a Screen Time Schedule: Settings → Screen Time → Screen Time Schedule.

**On iOS 26:**

1.  Open Settings → Screen Time → App Limits → Add Limit.
2.  Tap a category to see its apps, select TikTok, tap Next and set the time.

Apple notes that, by default, a limit can be ignored once it’s reached. With a Screen Time passcode set, Block at Downtime keeps apps closed during Downtime.

**The passcode:** Settings → Screen Time → Manage Screen Time → Lock Screen Time Settings (on iOS 26, Settings → Screen Time → Lock Screen Time Settings). If you set it yourself, you know it: [why your own passcode is easy to get around](https://habittoll.com/guides/screen-time-passcode/).

### 3. On Android: an app timer

1.  Open Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers.
2.  Tap Set timer next to TikTok, choose the time per day and tap OK.

When the time is up, TikTok closes and its icon dims for the rest of the day. Timers reset at midnight. So that the timer isn’t simply deleted, set a PIN: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App limits → App limits PIN. On a Samsung Galaxy the menus are named differently: [how to block apps on Android](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-android/) has both.

### 4. TikTok in the browser

- **TikTok’s own limit** follows your account to tiktok.com.
- **Android:** Digital Wellbeing has a separate site timer for Chrome. In Digital Wellbeing, tap the chart, then Chrome and Show sites, and tap Set site timer next to tiktok.com.
- **iPhone:** on iOS 27, a Time Allowance covers an app’s website when the app declares that website as its own. On iOS 26 you can block the address completely: Settings → Screen Time → Content & Privacy Restrictions → App Store, Media, Web, & Games → Web Content → Limit Adult Websites, then Add Website under Never Allow.

### When a limit is too easy to get past

If you keep typing the code or deleting the timer, a question with a price is a middle way:

- HabitToll asks “worth it?” before TikTok opens, and on iPhone before tiktok.com too.
- Walking away is one tap and free.
- Going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29; then it asks again.
- You can block always, or only at the times you pick, and give a group of apps, like TikTok and Instagram, free minutes a day or free hours.
- Its settings lock makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code.

### Which to use

| You want | Use |
|----|----|
| A reminder after a while on TikTok | TikTok’s Daily screen time |
| A daily amount that closes the app | Screen Time (iPhone) or an app timer (Android) |
| TikTok closed at night or at work | A Screen Time Schedule (Downtime on iOS 26), or Focus mode on Android |
| A decision at every open, not a countdown | HabitToll |

### Questions

#### What is the TikTok screen time passcode?

For adults, it’s the code TikTok shows on the screen when you reach your limit: type it to keep watching. There’s no secret code to remember. With Family Pairing, a parent gets a one-time code instead.

#### Why doesn’t my TikTok time limit stop me?

For adults it’s a reminder that the code on the screen gets you past. For a limit that closes the app, use Screen Time on iPhone or an app timer on Android, with a passcode or PIN that someone else keeps.

*Steps from TikTok’s support pages, Apple’s iPhone User Guide for iOS 27 and iOS 26, and Google’s Android help for Digital Wellbeing, checked on 17 October 2026. Menus can differ by app version, region and phone.*

## How to limit YouTube Shorts, or block YouTube, on iPhone and Android

https://habittoll.com/guides/limit-youtube-shorts/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/ratgeber/youtube-shorts-begrenzen/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/guias/limitar-youtube-shorts/

[Guide](https://habittoll.com/guides/) · Updated 17 October 2026

There’s no switch that turns Shorts off for adults. YouTube’s Shorts feed limit, which can even be set to zero, ends with a reminder you can dismiss, and Show fewer Shorts only shows fewer. Screen Time and Digital Wellbeing can limit the whole YouTube app, long videos included, but not Shorts alone; so does HabitToll, which asks before YouTube opens.

### 1. YouTube’s Shorts feed limit

1.  In the YouTube app, tap You, then Settings.
2.  Tap Time management → Shorts feed limit.
3.  Choose a time. Zero is one of the options.

When you reach it, a reminder appears; for adults it can be dismissed, and the limit ignored. Only on supervised kid and teen accounts does the limit stop Shorts scrolling for the rest of the day, set by a parent in Family Center.

### 2. Fewer Shorts on Home

On the Home feed, tap More (⋮) at the top of a row of Shorts and choose Show fewer Shorts. Fewer Shorts are recommended there; they don’t disappear. To undo it, go to My Activity → Other activity. Not interested and Don’t recommend channel tune the rest of what YouTube suggests.

Deleting your watch history and turning it off removes video recommendations from Home, YouTube says. What it does to the Shorts feed, YouTube doesn’t say.

### 3. Reminders to stop watching

In the app’s Settings, turn on Remind me to take a break, or Remind me when it’s bedtime. Both are off by default for adults.

### 4. Limit the whole YouTube app with the phone

- **iPhone, iOS 27:** Settings → Screen Time → Time Allowances. Tap the category YouTube counts toward and set its daily time; Manage Categories shows which apps each category holds.
- **iPhone, iOS 26:** Settings → Screen Time → App Limits → Add Limit. Tap a category, select YouTube, tap Next and set the time.
- **Android:** Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers. Tap Set timer next to YouTube, choose the time and tap OK.

These limit all of YouTube, long videos included: Apple and Google describe limits for apps, categories and websites, not for part of an app. A Screen Time passcode or an App limits PIN keeps the limit from being undone in a second: [how to block apps on iPhone](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-iphone/), [on Android, Samsung included](https://habittoll.com/guides/block-apps-on-android/).

### 5. YouTube in the browser

- **Android:** Digital Wellbeing has a separate site timer for Chrome. In Digital Wellbeing, tap the chart, then Chrome and Show sites, and tap Set site timer next to youtube.com.
- **iPhone:** on iOS 27, a Time Allowance covers an app’s website when the app declares that website as its own. On iOS 26 you can block youtube.com completely: Settings → Screen Time → Content & Privacy Restrictions → App Store, Media, Web, & Games → Web Content → Limit Adult Websites, then Add Website under Never Allow.

### When you want to decide each time

HabitToll asks “worth it?” before the YouTube app opens. Like the phone’s own tools, it works on the whole app, not on Shorts alone.

- Walking away is one tap and free.
- Going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29; then it asks again.
- You can block always, or only at the times you pick, and give a group of apps free minutes a day or free hours, like 20:00 to 21:00.
- On iPhone it can ask before youtube.com too.
- Its settings lock makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code.

### Which to use

| You want | Use |
|----|----|
| A nudge after a while of Shorts | YouTube’s Shorts feed limit |
| Fewer Shorts on Home | Show fewer Shorts |
| A daily amount for all of YouTube | Screen Time (iPhone) or an app timer (Android) |
| A decision every time YouTube opens | HabitToll |

### Questions

#### Can I turn off YouTube Shorts completely?

Not on an adult account, as of October 2026. A Shorts feed limit of zero shows a reminder you can dismiss, and Show fewer Shorts only reduces them. On supervised kid and teen accounts, a parent can set the Shorts limit to zero.

#### Can Screen Time block only Shorts and keep the rest of YouTube?

Not in a way Apple or Google describe: Screen Time and Digital Wellbeing limit apps, categories or websites, so a limit on YouTube covers all of YouTube, long videos included.

*Steps from YouTube Help, the YouTube blog, Apple’s iPhone User Guide for iOS 27 and iOS 26, and Google’s Android help for Digital Wellbeing, checked on 17 October 2026. Menus can differ by app version and phone.*

## The best app blockers for iPhone and Android in 2026

https://habittoll.com/compare/best-app-blockers/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/vergleich/beste-app-blocker/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/comparar/mejores-bloqueadores-de-apps/

[Comparison](https://habittoll.com/compare/) · Updated 17 October 2026

There’s no single best app blocker, because they limit apps in different ways: a daily amount and a schedule (Screen Time, Digital Wellbeing, Opal), a pause before the app opens (one sec, ScreenZen), a physical key (Brick), exercise (Pushscroll), or a question with a price (HabitToll). Here’s what each one does, what it costs and when it fits, with facts from the stores and the makers' own pages.

### At a glance

| App | How it limits | Price | Platforms |
|----|----|----|----|
| Screen Time (Apple) | A daily amount per category and a schedule; a passcode protects the settings | Free, part of iOS | iPhone, iPad, Mac |
| Digital Wellbeing (Google) | A daily timer per app, Focus mode and Bedtime mode | Free, part of Android | Android |
| Opal | Focus sessions, schedules, time and open limits; a strict Hard Mode in Pro | A free plan; Opal Pro $19.99 a month or $99.99 a year | iPhone, Android, Mac |
| one sec | A short pause, like a breath, before the app opens | Free for one app; one sec pro $6.99 a month, $19.99 a year or $99.99 once | iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android |
| ScreenZen | A wait before the app opens, which can get longer each time, plus open limits and schedules | Free; optional tips, no subscription | iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android, Windows |
| Brick | A physical block: tap your phone on it to block chosen apps, and again to unblock them | $59 for the device, no subscription | iPhone, Android (with NFC) |
| Pushscroll | You earn more time with push-ups, squats or steps | A subscription after a 7-day trial: $14.99 a month or $59.99 a year | iPhone, Android |
| Brainrot | Schedules, a focus timer and a brain avatar | A subscription, $3.99 to $49.99 depending on the plan | iPhone |
| HabitToll | Asks “worth it?” at each open: walk away for free, or buy 10 minutes at your price | Free to download, no subscription; 10 minutes from €0.29 | iPhone, Android |

US prices as listed on the App Store or the maker’s site; they differ by country.

### Which kind suits you

- **A daily amount, free and built in:** Screen Time on iPhone, Digital Wellbeing on Android.
- **Focus sessions and blocks you can’t end early:** Opal.
- **A moment to think before the app:** one sec or ScreenZen.
- **The phone locked until you’re back at one place:** Brick.
- **Scrolling you earn with exercise:** Pushscroll.
- **A decision at every open, paying only when an app is worth it:** HabitToll.

### The apps one by one

#### Screen Time

Built into every iPhone. On iOS 27, Time Allowances give categories like Social Media a daily amount and a Screen Time Schedule sets the hours; on iOS 26 the same tools are App Limits and Downtime. A Screen Time passcode stops quick changes, but if you set it yourself, you know it. [HabitToll vs Screen Time](https://habittoll.com/compare/screen-time/)

#### Digital Wellbeing

Built into Android. App timers give single apps a daily amount; when it runs out, the app closes and its icon dims until midnight. Focus mode pauses chosen apps on a schedule. [HabitToll vs Digital Wellbeing](https://habittoll.com/compare/digital-wellbeing/)

#### Opal

A focus app with sessions, schedules, time limits and open limits. Leaving a block early goes through a “Waiting Room”; Hard Mode in Opal Pro allows no unblocks except a weekly Emergency Pass. [HabitToll vs Opal](https://habittoll.com/compare/opal/)

#### one sec

Plays a short pause, like a breathing exercise, before a distracting app opens; then you choose. Free for one app; one sec pro covers more apps and adds stricter blocks. [HabitToll vs one sec](https://habittoll.com/compare/one-sec/)

#### ScreenZen

Makes you wait a few seconds before a distracting app opens, and the wait can get longer each time; it can also limit how many times a day an app opens, block on a schedule and set a daily screen-time budget. Free, supported by optional tips. [HabitToll vs ScreenZen](https://habittoll.com/compare/screenzen/)

#### Brick

A small NFC block you keep somewhere, like at home. Tap your phone on it to block the apps you chose, and tap it again to unblock them, so getting back in means going to the Brick. $59 for the device, with 5 Emergency Unbricks for when you can’t get to it. [HabitToll vs Brick](https://habittoll.com/compare/brick/)

#### Pushscroll

Time limits you top up with exercise: the camera counts push-ups or squats, or steps come from Apple Health. A subscription after a free week. [HabitToll vs Pushscroll](https://habittoll.com/compare/pushscroll/)

#### Brainrot

Blocks apps and websites on schedules or after a daily limit, with a focus timer and a brain avatar that decays while you scroll. iPhone only, with a subscription for all features. [HabitToll vs Brainrot](https://habittoll.com/compare/brainrot/)

#### HabitToll

Our app. Before an app you picked opens, it asks “worth it?” Walking away is one tap, free and counted; going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, from €0.29, as a one-time in-app purchase. No subscription, no ads, no account. A settings lock makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code.

### Questions

#### What is the best free app blocker?

Screen Time on iPhone and Digital Wellbeing on Android are free and built in. ScreenZen is free, with optional tips. one sec is free for one app. HabitToll is free to download, and walking away is always free; you pay only when you buy 10 minutes of an app.

#### Which app blocker is hardest to get around?

Brick, because unblocking needs the device itself, apart from 5 Emergency Unbricks. Opal’s Hard Mode allows no unblocks except a weekly Emergency Pass. Any app can still be deleted; [an app blocker you can’t just switch off](https://habittoll.com/guides/app-blocker-you-cant-turn-off/) covers the options.

*Facts checked on 16 and 17 October 2026 on the App Store (US and Germany), Google Play, the makers’ sites and help pages, and Apple’s and Google’s guides. Prices change and differ by country. HabitToll is our app, so we’re not neutral; if something here is out of date, write to help@habittoll.com.*

## HabitToll vs Screen Time on iPhone

https://habittoll.com/compare/screen-time/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/vergleich/bildschirmzeit/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/comparar/tiempo-de-uso/

[Comparison](https://habittoll.com/compare/) · Updated 16 October 2026

Screen Time is built into every iPhone and is free. On iOS 27 it gives categories like Social Media a daily Time Allowance and sets hours with a Screen Time Schedule; on iOS 26 the same tools are App Limits and Downtime. HabitToll uses Apple’s Screen Time system underneath, but instead of a countdown it asks “worth it?” each time, and going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set.

### At a glance

|  | Screen Time | HabitToll |
|----|----|----|
| What it is | Apple’s built-in tool: Time Allowances, a Screen Time Schedule and usage reports | An app blocker that asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open |
| Price | Free, part of iOS | Free to download, no subscription; 10-minute unlocks at a price you set, from €0.29 |
| How it limits | A daily amount per category, and the hours when apps can be used | A question at each open: walk away for free, or buy 10 minutes |
| What you limit | A daily total and categories on iOS 27; categories or single apps with App Limits on iOS 26 | Single apps and websites you pick |
| Getting past it | Change the settings, unless a Screen Time passcode protects them | Pay your price; 2 free emergency unlocks a month |
| Protecting the settings | A four-digit Screen Time passcode | A settings lock: easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code |
| Usage reports | Yes, detailed | Your walk-aways, streak and monthly bill |
| Platforms | iPhone, iPad, Mac | iPhone (iOS 26.4 or later) and Android (8 or later) |

### The main difference

Screen Time counts minutes. Apps in a category work until their allowance runs out, and a schedule decides when they can be used at all. Without a passcode you can change all of it in a few taps, and Apple notes that on iOS 26 a limit can be ignored once it’s reached unless you block it. With a passcode someone else keeps, Screen Time becomes a hard stop.

HabitToll asks each time you open an app you picked, outside any free minutes or free hours you gave it. Walking away is one tap, free, and counted; going in costs a price you chose, so a quick scroll becomes a small purchase you decide on. The price can double with each unlock on the same day, if you turn that on, and a monthly limit makes HabitToll ask before every paid unlock past it.

### When Screen Time is the better fit

- You want a hard daily cap, and someone else can keep the passcode.
- You want detailed reports across iPhone, iPad and Mac.
- You don’t want to pay anything, ever.

### When HabitToll is the better fit

- You keep giving yourself more time, but a hard block feels too strict.
- You want each open to be a decision, not a countdown.
- You want a lock that works on your own: HabitToll’s settings lock can make easier changes wait 24 hours, or need a partner’s code if you’d like one.
- You also use Android.

### Using both

They work together. HabitToll uses Apple’s Screen Time framework to block the apps you pick, and you can keep Screen Time’s reports and schedule alongside it.

### Questions

#### Does HabitToll need Screen Time to be on?

HabitToll asks for Screen Time access during setup; that’s how iOS lets an app block other apps. Your own Screen Time settings and reports stay as they are.

#### Can Screen Time charge for unlocks?

No. Screen Time has no payments. Putting a price on 10 minutes is what HabitToll adds.

*Facts checked on 16 October 2026 in Apple’s iPhone User Guide for iOS 27 and iOS 26, and on the App Store. HabitToll is our app, so we’re not neutral; if something here is out of date, write to help@habittoll.com.*

## HabitToll vs Digital Wellbeing on Android

https://habittoll.com/compare/digital-wellbeing/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/vergleich/digital-wellbeing/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/comparar/bienestar-digital/

[Comparison](https://habittoll.com/compare/) · Updated 16 October 2026

Digital Wellbeing is Google’s free tool on Android: an app timer closes an app for the rest of the day once its time is used up, and Focus mode pauses apps during set hours. HabitToll asks “worth it?” each time you open an app you picked, and going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set.

### At a glance

|  | Digital Wellbeing | HabitToll |
|----|----|----|
| What it is | Google’s tool on Android: app timers, Focus mode, Bedtime mode and usage reports | An app blocker that asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open |
| Price | Free, part of Android | Free to download, no subscription; 10-minute unlocks at a price you set, from €0.29 |
| How it limits | A daily timer per app; when it runs out, the app closes and its icon dims until midnight | A question at each open: walk away for free, or buy 10 minutes |
| Getting past it | Delete or change the timer, use Take a break in Focus mode, or turn Focus mode off | Pay your price; 2 free emergency unlocks a month |
| Protecting the settings | An optional four-digit PIN for app timers | A settings lock: easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code |
| Usage reports | Yes, a usage dashboard | Your walk-aways, streak and monthly bill |
| Platforms | Android | Android (8 or later) and iPhone (iOS 26.4 or later) |

### The main difference

Digital Wellbeing works with time. A timer runs down, the app closes, and it stays closed until midnight. Without a PIN, you can delete the timer in the same screen where you set it. With the App limits PIN on, changing a timer needs the PIN, but a PIN you choose yourself is one you know.

HabitToll works with decisions. Each open of an app you picked asks “worth it?”, outside any free minutes or free hours you set. Walking away is free and counted; going in costs a price you chose, which can double with each unlock that day if you turn that on. The settings lock doesn’t need anyone else: easier changes, like removing an app or lowering the price, can simply wait 24 hours.

### When Digital Wellbeing is the better fit

- A daily timer is all you want, and you’ll leave it alone, or someone else can keep the PIN.
- You want Bedtime mode at night, with Do Not Disturb and a greyscale screen.
- You don’t want to pay anything, ever.

### When HabitToll is the better fit

- You keep deleting the timer when it runs out.
- You’d rather decide at each open than run out of minutes.
- You want a lock that works on your own: a 24-hour wait, or a partner’s code if you’d like one.
- You also have an iPhone, or friends who do.

### Using both

They work side by side. You can keep Bedtime mode and the usage dashboard, and let HabitToll ask in front of the apps you open without thinking.

### Questions

#### Does HabitToll replace Digital Wellbeing?

No. It adds a question and a price in front of the apps you pick. Digital Wellbeing stays on your phone with its reports.

#### What does HabitToll see on Android?

Usage access shows HabitToll which app is in front. Which apps you block, and how long you use them, never leave your phone.

*Facts checked on 16 October 2026 in Google’s Android and Pixel help for Digital Wellbeing. Menus can differ on phones from other makers. HabitToll is our app, so we’re not neutral; if something here is out of date, write to help@habittoll.com.*

## HabitToll vs Opal

https://habittoll.com/compare/opal/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/vergleich/opal/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/comparar/opal/

[Comparison](https://habittoll.com/compare/) · Updated 16 October 2026

Both use Apple’s Screen Time to block apps on iPhone, and both are on Android. Opal is a focus app with sessions, schedules, time limits and a strict Hard Mode in its Pro subscription; HabitToll asks “worth it?” each time and lets you buy 10 minutes at a price you set, or walk away for free, with no subscription.

### At a glance

|  | Opal | HabitToll |
|----|----|----|
| What it is | A screen time app for blocking apps and websites: focus sessions, schedules, time limits and open limits | An app blocker that asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open |
| Price | A free plan with limits; Opal Pro is a subscription, $19.99 a month or $99.99 a year on the US App Store | Free to download, no subscription; 10-minute unlocks at a price you set, from €0.29 |
| When you open a blocked app | A block screen; if your rule allows unblocks, you wait through a “Waiting Room” first, like a pause, a breathing exercise or a small game | “Worth it?”: walk away for free, or buy 10 minutes |
| Getting past a block | Unblock after the Waiting Room; in Hard Mode (Pro) no unblocks, only an Emergency Pass once a week for an hour | Pay your price; 2 free emergency unlocks a month |
| Platforms | iPhone (iOS 18 or later), Android, Mac | iPhone (iOS 26.4 or later) and Android (8 or later) |
| Account | Needed to use Pro on more than one device | None |
| App Store privacy label | Data used to track you: identifiers. Data linked to you: purchases, contact info, user content, identifiers, usage data | Data linked to you: purchase history and a user ID, for the app’s features. Nothing used to track you |

### The main difference

Opal is built around focus time: you set rules, and inside them apps are blocked. Getting out early goes through a waiting room, and in Pro’s Hard Mode there’s no way out except a weekly Emergency Pass. It’s thorough, with reports, a focus score and sounds for working.

HabitToll is built around the single open. Each time you open an app you picked, it asks “worth it?”, outside any free minutes or free hours you set. Walking away is one tap, free and counted; going in costs 10 minutes at a price you chose. There’s no subscription and no plan to upgrade to: everything is included, and you pay only for the minutes you decide are worth it.

### When Opal is the better fit

- You want deep-focus sessions with a timer, sounds and a focus score.
- You want blocks you really can’t end early, and you’re fine paying for Pro.
- You use a Mac as well.

### When HabitToll is the better fit

- You’d rather decide at each open than plan focus sessions.
- You’d rather pay a small price, chosen by you, than a subscription.
- You want no account and as little data as possible.

### Questions

#### Is there an Opal alternative without a subscription?

HabitToll has no subscription and no paid plan. It’s free to download; you pay only when you buy 10 minutes of an app, at a price you set, from €0.29. Walking away is always free.

#### Does HabitToll have a hard mode?

Not in Opal’s sense. HabitToll’s settings lock makes easier changes wait 24 hours or need a partner’s code, so you can’t undo your rules in the moment, but there’s always a way in: paying your price, or one of two free emergency unlocks a month.

## HabitToll vs one sec

https://habittoll.com/compare/one-sec/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/vergleich/one-sec/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/comparar/one-sec/

[Comparison](https://habittoll.com/compare/) · Updated 16 October 2026

Both put a moment of friction in front of an app instead of a hard wall. one sec makes you take a short pause first, like a deep breath, and then you decide; HabitToll asks “worth it?” and going in costs 10 minutes at a price you set, while walking away is free.

### At a glance

|  | one sec | HabitToll |
|----|----|----|
| What it is | A short pause before distracting apps open: a breathing exercise or another quick task, then you choose | An app blocker that asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open |
| Price | Free for one app; one sec pro for more apps: $6.99 a month, $19.99 a year or $99.99 once on the US App Store, with a one-week trial | Free to download, no subscription; 10-minute unlocks at a price you set, from €0.29 |
| When you open a limited app | The pause plays first; after it, you can open the app or leave | “Worth it?”: walk away for free, or buy 10 minutes |
| After a while in the app | It can ask again after a set time (re-intervention) | Your 10 minutes run; then it asks again |
| Getting past it | Sit through the pause, then open the app; one sec pro adds strict blocks for harder limits | Pay your price; 2 free emergency unlocks a month |
| Platforms | iPhone, iPad, Mac and Android, plus a Safari extension for websites | iPhone (iOS 26.4 or later) and Android (8 or later) |
| App Store privacy label | Data not linked to you: usage data, for analytics | Data linked to you: purchase history and a user ID, for the app’s features |

### The main difference

one sec adds time: a few seconds of breathing before the app opens. The pause gives you a moment to notice what you’re doing, and then the choice is yours.

HabitToll adds a price. The question is the same, “do I really want this?”, but saying yes costs something you chose yourself, so a quick scroll becomes a small purchase. Walking away is one tap, free and counted, and the price can double with each unlock on the same day, if you turn that on.

### When one sec is the better fit

- A pause is enough for you, and you don’t want money involved.
- You want it on iPad and Mac too.
- One app is all you want to limit, and you’d like that free.

### When HabitToll is the better fit

- You’ve learned to wait out a pause, and need something that costs more than a few seconds.
- You’d rather pay per unlock, at a price you choose, than a subscription.
- You want a streak and a monthly bill that show what each open cost.

### Questions

#### Is there a one sec alternative without a subscription?

HabitToll has no subscription. It’s free to download; you pay only when you buy 10 minutes of an app, at a price you set, from €0.29. Walking away is always free.

#### Can I use both?

Yes, though two pauses in front of the same app is a lot. One per app is usually enough.

## HabitToll vs Pushscroll

https://habittoll.com/compare/pushscroll/ · German: https://habittoll.com/de/vergleich/pushscroll/ · Spanish: https://habittoll.com/es/comparar/pushscroll/

[Comparison](https://habittoll.com/compare/) · Updated 16 October 2026

Both put something in front of the apps you open too often. Pushscroll makes you earn app time with exercise, counted by the camera, or with your steps; HabitToll asks “worth it?” and lets you buy 10 minutes at a price you set, or walk away for free. Pushscroll needs a subscription after its trial; HabitToll has none.

### At a glance

|  | Pushscroll | HabitToll |
|----|----|----|
| What it is | Time limits on apps; you earn more time with push-ups, squats and other exercises, or with steps from Apple Health | An app blocker that asks “worth it?” before the apps you pick open |
| Price | A subscription after a 7-day free trial: $14.99 a month or $59.99 a year (US prices on pushscroll.com) | Free to download, no subscription; 10-minute unlocks at a price you set, from €0.29 |
| When your time is up | Exercise to earn more minutes; the camera counts the reps | “Worth it?”: walk away for free, or buy 10 minutes |
| Platforms | iPhone (iOS 16 or later) and Android | iPhone (iOS 26.4 or later) and Android (8 or later) |
| Account | Not needed | None |
| App Store privacy label | Data used to track you: purchases, identifiers. Data linked to you: health and fitness, purchases, contact info, identifiers, usage data, diagnostics | Data linked to you: purchase history and a user ID, for the app’s features. Nothing used to track you |

### The main difference

Pushscroll turns screen time into exercise: “One pushup = one minute of app time”, in its own words. If you like moving and want a reason to, that’s a strong idea.

HabitToll turns each open into a decision. You pick a price for 10 minutes when you set it up; when an app is worth it, you pay and go in, and when it isn’t, walking away is one tap and counts. There’s no exercise, no camera and no subscription: you only pay for the minutes you decide are worth it.

### When Pushscroll is the better fit

- You want to move more, and exercise is a reward you’ll actually do.
- You’re fine with a subscription.

### When HabitToll is the better fit

- You can’t or don’t want to do exercises whenever you want an app: on the bus, in bed, at work.
- You’d rather pay a small price, chosen by you, than a monthly subscription.
- You’d rather not use the camera or Apple Health for it.

### Questions

#### Is HabitToll a free alternative to Pushscroll?

HabitToll is free to download and has no subscription. Blocking and walking away are free; you pay only when you buy 10 minutes, at a price you set, from €0.29.

#### Does HabitToll use the camera?

No. HabitToll never uses the camera.
